Now, focus on the member functions at the top of the file. We will be overriding and/or implementing the CPlugin functions for our synth projects:

## Standard plug-in-Functions:

Here you see the constructor and destructor, which we use to initialize variables and destroy objects.

```cpp
CMiniSynth():
  allocate dynamic memory
  initialize variables
```

```cpp
virtual ~CMiniSynth():
  deallocate any allocated memory
```

```cpp
virtual bool __stdcall prepareForPlay():
  the-per run initialization function
  always set the sample rate on sub-components
  always update the synth objects
```

```cpp
virtual bool __stdcall processAudioFrame(float* pInputBuffer,
  float* pOutputBuffer,
  UINT uNumInputChannels,
  UINT uNumOutputChannels);
```

```cpp
virtual bool __stdcall userInterfaceChange(int nControlIndex):
  this is where we render the synthesized audio output
  this is called after the user moves a control on the GUI; you may optionally do not processing here: in all cases we will call the synth updating function
```

## MIDI and Joystick Control Functions

Table 2.3 lists the MIDI functions we will implement, and you can find their prototypes in the area marked "Advanced Functions." In the VectorSynth and AniSynth, we will use the vector joystick, which issues location and mixing information. That method is also in this group of functions:

```cpp
virtual bool __stdcall joystickControlChange(float fControlA,
  float fControlB,
  float fControlC,
  float fControlD,
  float fACMix,
  float fBDMMix);
```

- Indicates the user has moved the built-in vector joystick which we use in VectorSynth
- AniSynth

```cpp
<SNIP SNIP SNIP> -- you can skip functions 8 and 9
virtual bool __stdcall midiNoteOn(UINT uchannel,
                               UINT uMIDINote,
                               UINT velocity);
```

- called for each MIDI note event delivering channel, note number and velocity

```cpp
virtual bool __stdcall midiNoteOff(UINT uchannel, UINT uMIDINote,
                                      UINT velocity, bool bAllNotesOff);
```

- called for each MIDI note off event
- also called for all notes off panic message

```cpp
virtual bool __stdcall midiModWheel(UINT uchannel, UINT uModValue);
- function to handle changes to the Mod Wheel (found on most synth controllers)
```

```cpp
virtual bool __stdcall midiPitchBend(UINT uchannel,
                                       int nActualPitchValue,
                                       float nNormalizedPitchBendValue);
```

- specialized function for the pitch bend wheel/joystick

- all the rest of the MIDI messages including continuous controllers


```cpp

double m_dLastNoteFrequency;
```

```cpp
// --- our receive channel
UINT m_uMidiRxChannel;
```

The synthesizer's polyphony is maintained by maintaining an array of voice pointer objects. This array is named m_pVoiceArray for all the synths. The difference is in the kind of pointers they hold; in this case the array holds Synth pointers. The three functions below its definition are for handling the time ordering of the voices. The update() function is for updating all the synth variables at once. We will get into the details of these as well as the few remaining variables as Chapters 3–12 progress.

Now, let's look at each function implementation by-one. The synth projects are all very similar from the plug-in object's point of view. Most of the work that differentiates the synths is done in the CVoice objects that we will design. So, once you understand one synth, the others are very easy to grasp. Open the MiniSynth.cpp file, and let's start at the top and work our down through the implementation.

## constructor

The constructor in each RackAFX plug-in does the following:

- allocate dynamic memory
- initialize variables
- deallocate any allocated memory
- the-per run initialization function
- always set the sample rate on sub-components
- always update the synth objects
- render the synthesized audio output
- this is called after the user moves a control on the GUI; you may optionally do not processing here: in all cases we will call the synth updating function

The synthesizer's polyphony is maintained by maintaining an array of voice pointer objects. This array is named m_pVoiceArray for all the synths. The difference is in the kind of pointers they hold; in this case the array holds Synth pointers. The three functions below its definition are for handling the time ordering of the voices. The update() function is for updating all the synth variables at once. We will get into the details of these as well as the few remaining variables as Chapters 3–12 progress.
